title: Promoters and nightlife in Lake Charles and the Louisiana-Texas circuit
summary: Tex recalls Frank Painia and Charlie Rosenthal, Lake Charles clubs, the hucklebuck, Southern University friends, and gathering news from bars.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I'm just curious stuff about Butch Curran, about the traveling, about writing the column and so forth. Go and put your date on it again and put your billboard on it.
Right, yeah, January the 10th, 1996, Real Number 3 with Tech Stevens.

And, you know, as we were saying, Ted, we were talking about writing columns and so forth, about knowing people, about getting involved, having the right kind of connection, so that you could get into the structure of putting something together to inform in a newspaper, because a lot of people call newspaper an organ. It's an organ of information. That's what a newspaper is. See, and I highlight, I was talking about Charlie Rosenthal over in Orange, Texas, who was a good friend of Frank Pannier. Both of them were very good promoters. And since the Dewdrop had developed an image factor worldwide right after World War II, because he brought in, Frank brought in so much live entertainment and so many other beautiful named people. And Frank Pannier brought in more great names of entertainment than anybody that I've ever seen in this city. And many a time, when they would finish working at the Dewdrop, Frank Pannier and Charlie Rosenthal would get together, and they would transport those people over to Orange, Texas. See, Charlie Rosenthal had, at that time, was known as a movie theater with an auditorium off on the side, where he would promote shows in and around Orange, Texas. So this is how Charlie Rosenthal and Frank Pannier got together. And then there was another guy in my travels over, and I was talking about going over through Louisiana, over in Lake Charles, which was one of my favorite cities in Louisiana, because Lake Charles had some of the prettiest women I had ever seen in my life. I came close to marrying an Indian black lady in Lake Charles before I married my wife, Marion, because that woman, even today, my wife may not like what I'm saying, but I think about that woman all the time, because, well, she impressed me as a young man at that particular time. And Andrew Robinson had this club called Club Raven, and there was a fellow, he and I were jazz buffs at that time, and we went to this with the Dizzy Gillespie thing, but we also had a great love for James Moody at that time, and we used to play Moody's Mood all night. You know, when I would get off from work, I was promoting liquor at that time, working for the liquor company, liquor and wine company, and sometimes Scoop Jones from New Orleans, who is now one of the outstanding sales representatives ever to come out of the city of New Orleans, who at that time was working for another liquor company, and he and I would meet up all across the state of Louisiana, sometimes in Texas or wherever we would go. And so, like I was saying, over in Lake Charles, they had Booger Red had a place across the street from the Raven, and Booger Red really promoted a lot of entertainment, because I can remember one week when I was in Lake Charles, if memory serves me correct, I think that's where our first, Jimmy Liggins played a hucklebuck, and that was, incidentally, a hucklebuck became a dance among black people, you know, and then eventually in New Orleans, it became a snowball. A lot of people didn't know that. It was a snowball called a hucklebuck, and it was discussed on the radio, just right in WWO radio just a couple of days ago with Andre Trevino, I wanted to call her, let her know, that hucklebuck before it was a snowball was a dance. That was a little bit before her time, too, because I was...
Her daddy would have known, though.

Your father would have known. And so, from Lake Charles, we went to Opelousas and to many other people, because, like I said, they had a lot of friends over there, like Ike Williamson, and then I had Tooney Forkard, who was a big-time gambler, who had a club in Lake Charles called The Arrow. Now, he promoted a lot of shows in the Lake Charles area, because, you see, I think I mentioned about the Army Air Force Base there in Lake Charles during World War II, and that had growth, given growth to Lake Charles, because, you know, you had a lot of those Air Force soldiers there.

And other businesses started developing around the area, so they brought a lot of money there. And so they had many good times there. And when I think about old Al Smith and Arthur Butte and Bill Kale and all those guys, and then it was Sergeant Henry Jett, who was the right-hand man to Lieutenant Flowers. I used to meet up with those guys on the main thoroughfare in Lake Charles. We used to have a lot of fun. And I used to get a lot of information from them whenever I would write a column. See, I wasn't only doing this for Butch Curry at the time, but I was also writing a column for the Informer Sentinel, which is also one of the oldest papers in Texas, a fellow by the name of Carter Wesley, who owned the Informer Sentinel. But he also had Informer Sentinels not only in Houston, had Informer Sentinels in Fort Worth, Informer Sentinels all over Texas, and in New Orleans and also in Baton Rouge at one time. So this is how I kept my contact, by staying close to the people in the various bars and lounges where I would navigate to from time to time, and people would pass information on to me. And this is how I got involved with a lot of people. You take friends like over in Appaloosias, Louisiana, we had a fellow by the name of Mason who probably had the largest black hotel ever in the history of Appaloosias. And a lot of people thought it was Louis Mason. But this guy's name, his first name was Mason, not Louis Mason, you see. And there was no relation. But eventually they developed a business thing between Louis Mason and Mason, I can't think of his last name, and Ferdinand Prout. They started this triumvirate, whereas people would leave New Orleans, and if they were traveling west, they would either stay in Appaloosias, or either they would stay at Mason's Hotel, or either they'd stay at Ferdinand Prout's Hotel here in New Orleans. And so blacks were really trying to accomplish some sort of business profile or connections by forming some amalgamation coming together. You know, so this is part of getting to know things, because when people find out that you work for a newspaper, you work for radio, they volunteer to give you quality information. You know, so I met quite a lot of people, and looking back at this column that I wrote for Butch Currier, Butch Currier back in 1953 for the Pittsburgh Courier. I think about a lot of people who passed on, and one of my fraternity brothers and very good friend, which I had a chance to stay in his house, passing through Baton Rouge years ago, was Dr. Felton G. Clark, who at that time was president of Southern University in Baton Rouge. That was before you had Southern in New Orleans and Southern in Shreveport. He took over from his father. Now, Felton G. Jr. was a very highly educated man who was very beautiful personality, and probably I regard as one of the world's great lecturers. I would love to listen to this man talk. I mean, he inspired me to do so many things because he was a counselor, even though I wasn't a student of Southern University, but Dr. Felton G. Clark through Prince Hall Masonic Lodge, which we all were members. And today, Prince Hall is the largest black fraternity on the face of the globe today. We have more money than any other black organization. And we've helped to generate money for the NAACP, for the Urban League, and for many other black organizations, which I'm very proud to say that I've done. And at that time, my very other good fraternity brother and good friend, Arnold W. Horst Mumford, one of the great football coaches of the 20th century who guided Southern University through its great football year of prominence back in the 40s and 50s. So, well, he's going to his great reward today, honored Horst Mumford. Tremendous M-U-M-F-O-R-D, Mumford. So he was a very, very great friend of mine also. And I really admired the man, I admired both men because they were in the field of education and they were trying to help young black people. Because whenever you can educate people, Tad, you're talking about building another taxpayer, another good citizen, another person that you could do, who's trustworthy, whether he or she be white or black, but they were proudly ingrained in the American way of living to expedite a new transition, to live by for unborn generations, for children to come. This is what life and living is all about. There's so many people that I've touched in my life as I think about the travels that I've had many years ago.
